notebook:
PLAN: Build a 9-column baseline separating saleable C3/C4 blends, pure iso-/n-pentane, C6 paraffin and naphthene blends, and pure C7/C8/C9; then inspect recoveries/costs and prune or upgrade the weakest columns. Step 1: baseline simulation.
Root cuts n-pentane from C6+. Light train cuts C4/C5, ethane/C3+, C3/C4 and iso/n-C5. Heavy train cuts C6 paraffins/MCP, cyclohexane/heptane, heptane/octane and octane/nonane. Moderate stages/reflux to gauge economics.

note: Prune every zero-value downstream branch, retaining only the three-column C4/C5 blend train.
notebook:
PLAN: Establish a profitable C4/C5-blend core, then optimize its three columns; only add further separations if incremental revenue clearly exceeds cost. Step 2: prune zero-value branches.
Root/T/TB earns $527.7M/yr from C4 and C5 blends. Removing TT and BB should leave root, T, TB and preserve those sales, with expected cost $363.6M and reward ~0.37. Root is very expensive ($261M); after pruning, test lower root severity and pressure drop while maintaining C5 purity. T and TB can also be tuned. Heavy-branch separations currently earn nothing and are unjustified.

note: Remove the entire zero-value heavy branch, leaving the three-column C4/C5 blend core.
notebook:
PLAN: Establish a profitable C4/C5-blend core, then optimize its three columns; only add further separations if incremental revenue clearly exceeds cost. Step 2: prune zero-value B branch and evaluate the minimal core.
Root/T/TB sells C4 for $116.7M and C5 for $350.7M, total $467.4M/yr. Selling B removes only its zero-value outputs and its $251.2M/yr cost; TT is already a leaf and needs no edit. Expected retained column cost is $363.6M/yr, giving reward about 0.236. Next reduce root severity (70 stages, reflux 4, cost $261.2M) while preserving the C4/C5 cut and TB purity. Other agents' tall C6 columns have produced no revenue and very high cost, so avoid that direction for now.

note: Reorder the same three separations: split C5 from C6 at the feed, then C4 from C5, then lights from the C4 blend. This should preserve revenue with a much warmer, cheaper root condenser.
notebook:
PLAN: Establish a profitable C4/C5-blend core, then optimize its columns; test a warmer C5/C6 root cut to avoid the very costly cold whole-feed C4/C5 split. Step 3: evaluate root C5/C6, T C4/C5, TT C3/C4.
Old direct sequence earns $467.4M and costs $363.6M; root alone costs $261.2M. New sequence should retain both blend revenues while moving the C5/C6 split to the root and making the cold C3/C4 column much smaller. All other branches are unsold. Avoid tall pure-C6 trains: visible attempts earn nothing and cost heavily.

note: Restore the proven blend core and make an intermediate root-cost reduction, avoiding the excessive overhead C5 leakage seen with 50 stages and reflux 3.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the proven $467.4M/yr C4/C5 blend core, then reduce root-column cost without losing the C4/C5 cut; only afterward tune downstream columns or try heat integration. Step 4: test a shorter, slightly lower-reflux root (60 stages, R=3.5, B=4, dp=0.2).
Proven core R239: root 70/4/4/0.2, T 50/2.5/2.5/0.1, TB 60/4/4/0.1 gives reward 0.237. Root costs $261.2M of $363.6M total. R243 shows aggressive reduction to 50/3/4 shifts too much N-pentane overhead and destroys C4 sales, so use an intermediate change. Reordered three-column train failed because no products met spec. Heavy branches have so far added cost without revenue.

note: Restore the profitable 60-stage blend core and test a deeper root pressure drop to reduce its dominant energy/refrigeration cost while retaining the same separation targets.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the proven $467M/yr C4/C5 blend core, reduce root-column cost without losing its cut, then tune downstream columns. Step 4: test 60/4/4 root at pressure drop 0.4 instead of 0.2.
R285 (60/4/4/0.2) restores reward 0.238 and revenue $467.2M; R239 (70 stages) is nearly identical. Root still costs $260.6M of $363.1M. A 50/3 root shifts too much C5 overhead and breaks C4 sales; boil-up 5.5 raises cost sharply. Higher root pressure drop may reduce pressure/refrigeration cost and improve volatility, but will be rejected if product purity collapses. Reordered train and heavy branches failed.

note: Restore the best blend core and reduce T boil-up to recover the large butane loss into TT, with slightly higher reflux to protect the C4 blend from light contamination.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the proven $467M/yr C4/C5 blend core, reduce product losses and column cost, then test a root side draw if tuning stalls. Step 5: reduce T reboil from 2.5 to 1.5 while raising reflux slightly, aiming to keep butanes out of TT.
R285 (60/4/4/0.2 root) gives reward 0.238, revenue $467.2M, cost $363.1M. Root costs $260.6M. Root dp 0.4 destroys C4/C5 cuts; dp 0.1 also fails. Heavy C6 branch failed. Main recoverable loss is TT: about 141 mol/s N-butane plus 63 isobutane, worth roughly $75-90M/yr as blend. TB already recovers essentially all C4/C5 fed to it. Lower T boil-up should shrink overhead and reduce cost; slight reflux increase should limit propane leakage into the C4 blend.

note: Test a sharper, higher-cut root to recover the large C5 loss into the unsold heavy bottoms, while retaining the proven downstream blend columns.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the proven $467M/yr C4/C5 blend core, reduce product losses and column cost, then test a root side draw if tuning stalls. Step 6: increase root stages and boil-up together to recover the roughly 300 mol/s C5 currently lost to B without dragging C6 overhead.
R285 (60/4/4/0.2 root) is best: reward 0.238, revenue $467.2M, cost $363.1M. Root costs $260.6M and loses about 300 mol/s C5 to B, worth about $250M/yr if recovered. Root dp 0.4 and 0.1 fail. T boil-up 1.5 destroys C5 purity despite recovering C4. TB 60/4/4 is essential; reduced duties fail. Heavy C6 branch failed. Test a sharper, higher-cut root (80/4/5), keeping proven downstream settings; added C5 revenue must outweigh extra root cost and any C6 leakage.

note: Restore R429 and recover the roughly 265 mol/s of pentane currently discarded in B with a C5/C6 splitter; this targets a large revenue stream without disturbing the proven C4/C5 core.
notebook:
PLAN: Build on R429’s best blend core, recover the valuable C5 lost in root bottoms with a dedicated C5/C6 column, then tune its duty and consider C6 recovery. Step 7: add B at 50/3/3/0.1.
R429: reward .243, revenue $464M, cost $358M. Root B is 2040 mol/s with about 265 mol/s N-pentane (13%) and C6+; recovering that C5 blend is worth roughly $230M/yr. Root boil-up 5 recovers C5 but overloads TB, destroys C4 blend purity, and adds $53M cost. Root dp .1/.4 and 80/4/5 fail; avoid these. T duty reductions fail. R429 TB 3.5/3.5 saves $5M over R285. Double effect gives no heat link and loses money. The new B column needs no deep refrigeration and should have a favorable value/cost balance.

note: Test a fundamentally cheaper two-column flowsheet: withdraw the C5 blend as a liquid side draw from the root and use the remaining column only to reject C3 and lighter material from the C4 blend.
notebook:
PLAN: Replace the three-column C4/C5 train with a root side-draw C5 cut and a single C3/C4 column; if purity is close, tune draw location/fraction. Step 8: test 60-stage root, liquid draw stage 40, f=.21.
Best prior core R480: .244, $464M revenue, $357M cost; root alone costs $260M. Added B C5 recovery failed (-.064) because B costs $135M and root still discards most C5 value. Root duty reductions destroy C5 purity. New structure should sell C5 directly from the root and C4 blend from T bottoms, eliminating the $43M TB column and reducing T feed/duty. Draw stage 40 is below feed to favour C5 over C4; f=.21 approximates the 695 mol/s C5 inventory.

note: Move the proven light-column liquid draw closer to the condenser so it rejects C4 and can qualify as a C3 blend, while preserving R529's profitable C4 bottoms.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore R529 and tune its light-column side draw upward to make a saleable C3 blend while retaining C4 bottoms. Step 9: move liquid draw from stage 20 to 10 at the same 0.55 fraction.
Best core R480 .244; R529 adds TT at only $17.6M and earns $43.7M C4, reaching .304. Its TTS is 71% C3 with 26% C4, so moving the draw 10 stages nearer the condenser should sharply reject butanes. Root heavy processing and side-draw C5 schemes have failed; do not repeat them. If C3 qualifies, tune fraction/stage for recovery; otherwise revert R529.

note: Copy R577's higher-recovery light column and split ethane from its clean C3 overhead, targeting a new saleable C3 blend without disturbing the profitable blend core.
notebook:
PLAN: Build on R577, the current best 0.321 plant. Add a small ethane/C3 splitter below TTT so its C3-rich bottoms become saleable; if this works, tune that splitter before attempting larger changes.
R577 retains more C4 than R529 and scores .321. Side draws at stages 10/20 and even 80 stages/reflux 8 never approach 95% C3, so stop pursuing a saleable TTS. TTT is 132 mol/s with 78% C3 and 22% ethane and no C4: a dedicated small column should readily produce >95% C3 bottoms. The unsold heavy B and earlier root changes were unprofitable; leave the proven core fixed.

note: Adopt the best island plant and add the proven small ethane/C3 splitter to monetize its clean C3-rich overhead, which should add substantially more revenue than column cost.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt R625's 0.422 four-column core (25% TT side draw), then recover its unsold C3-rich TTT overhead with a small ethane/C3 splitter; tune only if profitable.
R625's side draw is 97% C3 and earns $32.6M/yr, unlike the 45% draw. Its TTT is 182 mol/s, 83% C3 and 17% ethane with no C4, so a 40-stage splitter should yield saleable C3 bottoms. In my 45% version the same splitter earned $19.3M/yr for $8.3M/yr cost. Root/heavy-branch changes have consistently been unprofitable; keep that core fixed.

note: Reduce the ethane/C3 splitter to 24 stages and reflux/boil-up 2; propane and propylene need not be separated, so this should retain a clean C3 bottoms product at lower cost.
notebook:
PLAN: Keep the proven R625 blend core; first cheapen the profitable ethane/C3 splitter, then test a slightly sharper/larger TT side draw, and finally consider one cached-root energy reduction if budget permits.
Current best is 0.461. TTT adds $26.7M/yr revenue for $9.5M/yr; its only difficult requirement is removing ethane, since propane/propylene sell together. A 24-stage, R=B=2 column should suffice and save cost. TT at 25% draw produces 97% C3 side and exactly 95% C4 bottoms; modest draw increases risk losing the $69M C4 stream. Root changes propagate and cost five solves; R674 showed reflux reduction alone ruins the cut.

note: Adopt R717 and reduce only TTT boil-up from 1.5 to 1.0, aiming to retain its clean C3 bottoms while recovering more propane and propylene from the unsold overhead.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt R717's 0.479 core and optimize its small ethane/C3 splitter by lowering boil-up in steps; then use remaining solves for one high-value root-cost or side-draw experiment.
R717 gains $5.5M revenue and saves $1.1M versus my 24/2/2 splitter. At boil-up 1.5 it sends only 50 mol/s overhead (31.5 ethane, 18.5 C3), so reducing boil-up should recover more C3 while the 40 stages/3 reflux preserve ethane rejection. All four other columns and the C4/C5 products are proven and will remain cached. Avoid stronger/larger TTT settings: R719/R720 cost more without improving reward. Root is $260M but changes require five solves and prior root changes damaged the cut.

note: Trim the C4/C5 splitter from 60 stages and 3.5 reflux/boil-up to 40 and 2.5. Both products currently have roughly 99% blend purity, so substantial operating and capital savings should be available without losing sales.
notebook:
PLAN: Keep the proven 0.488 light-end/root core and use remaining solves to trim the oversized, one-solve C4/C5 splitter first; then optimize TT/T if purity margin remains.
TB is a $43M/yr column yet both outlets are about 99% blend, far above the 95% requirement. Reducing 60/3.5/3.5 to 40/2.5/2.5 should cut capital and duties substantially while preserving the near-equimolar C4/C5 split. This changes only TB, so it costs one solve. TTT boil-up 1.0 is optimal among tested 1.0/1.2/1.5; 30/2/1 was slightly worse. Root stage trimming saved almost nothing because its $260M cost is duty-dominated. Avoid adding heavy-bottom columns: previous attempt was strongly negative.

note: Restore R815, the best valid plant shown, after the aggressive C4/C5 splitter trim destroyed both blend specifications.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the best available blend core (R815), then use remaining solves only on small, isolated duty reductions with adequate product-purity margin.
The 40/2.5/2.5 TB experiment failed badly: both C4 and C5 products fell below 95%, so TB requires roughly 60 stages and 3.5 reflux/boil-up. R815 improves the best design to 0.492 by lowering TTT boil-up to 0.8; its C3 bottoms remains clean. Root stage reduction saves almost nothing, root boil-up increases are uneconomic, and the attempted double effect has no heat link and much higher cost. Avoid heavy-bottom columns and major root changes. Next candidates are modest TTT boil-up/reflux reductions, then small TT or T duty trims only if purity remains safe.

note: Test TTT boil-up 0.7 between the profitable 0.8 case and the failed 0.6 case, seeking extra C3 recovery and lower duty while keeping ethane below 5% in the bottoms.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the best available blend core (R815), then use remaining solves only on small, isolated duty reductions with adequate product-purity margin.
The 40/2.5/2.5 TB experiment failed badly: both C4 and C5 products fell below 95%, so TB requires roughly 60 stages and 3.5 reflux/boil-up. R815 improves the best design to 0.492 by lowering TTT boil-up to 0.8; its C3 bottoms remains clean. Root stage reduction saves almost nothing, root boil-up increases are uneconomic, and the attempted double effect has no heat link and much higher cost. Avoid heavy-bottom columns and major root changes. TTT boil-up 0.6 fails because ethane reaches 6% of its C3 bottoms; now testing the intermediate 0.7, which may retain >95% C3 while improving recovery and cost.

note: Combine the best TTT boil-up of 0.7 with R864's proven 45-stage root, retaining all downstream settings and seeking a small cost saving without changing product quality.
notebook:
PLAN: Preserve the 0.493 blend core, apply the proven 45-stage root saving, then use remaining solves only for isolated duty reductions with purity margin.
TTT boil-up 0.7 gives the best 0.493 result. R864 proves that a 45-stage root retains all blend products at TTT 0.8 and saves about $0.3M/yr, so combine it with 0.7. TB must remain 60/3.5/3.5: 40/2.5/2.5 failed badly. Avoid root pressure and boil-up changes, heavy-bottom columns, and double effect; all tested worse. Root stage reduction below 45 previously saved almost nothing, so further optimization should focus on modest reflux/duty changes only if products remain qualified.

note: Use the independently demonstrated TTT boil-up of 0.65: it keeps the C3 blend at specification, recovers slightly more C3, and reduces reboiler duty without disturbing any other column.
notebook: PLAN: Preserve the 0.494 blend core and use the final solves only for isolated, bracketed duty reductions with demonstrated purity margin. Set TTT boil-up to 0.65: R954 shows this retains a 95% C3 bottoms blend, increases C3 recovery slightly, and lowers TTT cost by about $0.3M/yr. TB remains 60/3.5/3.5 because aggressive trimming destroyed both blends; root remains 45/4/4/0.2. Avoid root reflux/pressure and heavy-bottom changes, which performed worse. After this safe improvement, consider only a very small additional isolated saving if enough solves remain.

note: Adopt R995's proven 0.529 plant and apply the validated TTT boil-up of 0.65, which should preserve the C3 blend while adding a small recovery and duty improvement.
notebook: PLAN: Adopt R995's proven 0.529 root-reflux 3.8 configuration, then apply the independently validated TTT boil-up 0.65 to gain its small duty/recovery benefit. With three solves left, this copy needs only one new TTT solve. Preserve all other columns. If successful, use at most one final solve on a modest TTT-only cost trim; avoid any root, TT, or TB change because their downstream columns would exceed the remaining budget.
